newsitem.title: FRANCE: French book reveals missed Mideast peace openings.
newsitem.headline: French book reveals missed Mideast peace openings.

text.p: As the Middle East teeters on the brink of another confrontation over Jerusalem, a book published in France on Wednesday offers new glimpses of missed opportunities for Arab-Israeli peace.
"Paix ou Guerres" (Peace or Wars) by long-serving French television Jerusalem correspondent Charles Enderlin calls itself a history of secret Arab-Israeli negotiations from 1917 to 1997.

Among its "scoops" is a report that Egypt invited the head of Israel's Mossad espionage agency to meet president Gamal Abdel Nasser in 1966 -- a year before the 1967 Middle East war -- but Israeli leaders turned the offer down, fearing a trap.
Enderlin says Mossad chief Meir Amit met a senior Egyptian intelligence officer in Geneva and was invited to Cairo.
But Amit's predecessor and rival, Isser Harel, convinced a hesitant prime minister Levi Eshkol that the Mossad chief might be abducted or tortured and the invitation was spurned.

However, historians may question the author's conclusion that "such a secret dialogue between the two countries could have prevented the series of misunderstandings which led the region to war the following year."
As the French philosopher Pascal observed: "Had Cleopatra's nose been shorter, the whole history of the world would have been different."

Enderlin says King Hussein of Jordan secretly visited Tel Aviv in late September 1973 to tip off Israeli prime minister Golda Meir that Syrian troops were on high alert for a possible attack on the occupied Golan Heights.
But Israeli military chiefs played down the warning two weeks before Syria and Egypt launched a joint attack on the Jewish state, catching the Israeli army by surprise.

He also discloses that Israeli internal security chiefs held secret talks with Palestine Liberation Organisation officials in Paris in 1985-86, a year before the Palestinian uprising broke out in the occupied West Bank and Gaza Strip.
In the contacts, PLO representatives accepted the idea of a gradual move to Palestinian self-government starting in Gaza.

The talks explored a possible political settlement but broke down when the Shin Bet security chiefs were forced to resign in a scandal over the killing of Palestinian bus hijackers, and prime minister Yitzhak Shamir decided not to renew the contacts.
Once again, Enderlin contends that an historic opportunity to avoid another round of Middle East bloodletting was lost.

He goes on to report that Yitzhak Rabin corresponded secretly with the PLO before the 1992 Israeli general election which brought his Labour party to power and led to the 1993 Israeli-Palestinian peace agreement.
However word of the contacts were leaked to a French weekly and the Israelis were forced to halt the contacts.
Enderlin also offers intriguing details of U.S. secretary of state James Baker's marathon shuttle to bring Israel and Palestinian representatives to the 1991 Madrid Middle East peace conference.
Baker gave his version of the inside story in his memoirs, but Enderlin quotes verbatim transcripts of the secretary's meetings with Palestinian leaders in Jerusalem.
At one point, he quotes Baker as telling them in anger over PLO leader Yasser Arafat: "Your clowns in Tunis are leading you to disaster. You are going to lose everything."
He warned the Palestinians they could miss perhaps the last opportunity to prevent Israel taking over the West Bank completely and forever.
Enderlin also quotes Baker as telling the Palestinians: "I'm going to tell you something very secret: the reason why members of Congress are elected is because they vote for Israel.
"The Israeli lobby is the richest and most powerful political lobby in America. That is where members of Congress get the money for their re-election."

Baker's warning that Washington could not and would not force Israel to end its occupation or stop settlements is topical this week, as Israeli security forces guard bulldozers starting a new Jewish housing project on captured land in East Jerusalem, putting Middle East peace to another severe test.
